title: Whole-number division and remainders

primary_objective.statement: Work out a whole-number quotient (//) and a remainder (%) for non-negative whole numbers, and use a remainder of 0 to spot an even split.

teach.text: When a program divides whole numbers it can keep two parts: how many whole times the divisor fits (the quotient) and what is left over (the remainder). In Python the quotient is written with // and the remainder with %.
To find them, ask how many whole times the divisor fits, multiply back, and subtract. The remainder is always smaller than the divisor; if it is not, the divisor fits at least once more.
A remainder of 0 means the division comes out even. That is how programs test for even numbers: a number % 2 is 0 when it is even and 1 when it is odd.

examples.text: 23 // 4: 4 fits into 23 five whole times (4 × 5 = 20), so the quotient is 5.
23 % 4: after taking 20 away, 3 is left over, so the remainder is 3.

alternate_explanations.text: Think of sharing sweets equally among friends with nothing cut in half. Each friend's share is the quotient; the sweets nobody gets are the remainder.

checks.feedback: 6 fits into 38 six whole times (6 × 6 = 36), so 38 // 6 is 6.
6 × 6 = 36 and 38 − 36 = 2, so the remainder is 2. 6 is the quotient, not the remainder.
10 fits into 50 exactly five times with nothing left, so 50 % 10 is 0.
9 does not fit into 7 even once, so the quotient is 0 (and 7 % 9 is 7).

misconceptions.label: giving the quotient when the remainder was asked for
misconceptions.contrast: // answers how many whole times the divisor fits; % answers what is left after that. Work out the quotient first, multiply back, and the difference is the remainder.

misconceptions.label: giving the decimal answer of ordinary division
misconceptions.contrast: % never gives a decimal. It is the whole amount left over, always smaller than the divisor.

return_cue: Back to your lesson: // keeps the whole times it fits, % keeps what is left over.
